blogs.title: Intrinsic, Not Propensity? The Eighth Circuit’s Broad View of Prior Gun Possession Evidence
blogs.description: This post would examine the panel’s treatment of testimony that Cutbank had been seen with the same sawed-off rifle before the charged incident. It would analyze how the Eighth Circuit continues to use the “intrinsic evidence” label to keep same-weapon possession evidence outside Rule 404(b), why that matters in felon-in-possession cases, and the doctrinal tension between this approach and broader efforts to cabin propensity-like evidence.

blogs.title: Context Without Constraint: Police-Testimony Hearsay, Later Confrontation, and the Minimal Role of Limiting Instructions
blogs.description: This post would focus on the court’s rejection of Cutbank’s request for an early limiting instruction regarding D.F.’s statements to police. It would explore the increasingly common move of admitting out-of-court statements as “context” for officer conduct, the court’s reliance on the fact that the declarant later testified, and what the opinion suggests about the practical limits of Confrontation Clause and hearsay objections at trial.

blogs.title: Harmless Error as Appellate Gravity: What Cutbank Says About Evidentiary Appeals in the Eighth Circuit
blogs.description: This post would analyze the opinion as a study in appellate method rather than substantive evidence law: undeveloped briefing, highly deferential abuse-of-discretion review, and a fallback to harmless error because the government’s proof was overwhelming. It would also discuss the panel’s unusual aside criticizing the government for unnecessarily expanding the issues on appeal, offering lessons for both defense and government advocates.

blogs.title: ACCA, Relevant Conduct, and the Parsimony Principle: Why a Four-Level Firearm Enhancement Still Counts
blogs.description: This post would unpack the sentencing holding, especially the interaction between ACCA status under § 924(e), the Armed Career Criminal guideline, and the separate § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) enhancement for possessing a gun in connection with another felony offense. It would consider the defendant’s argument that layering uncharged conduct onto an already severe ACCA sentence conflicts with § 3553(a)’s parsimony command, and explain why the panel treated that concern as a variance argument rather than a Guidelines-calculation problem.
